passage: Chaitanya saw it start at the bus stand in Hassan. Pradeep held out his phone to the group. 'Look what Sameer sent me. Rude or not?' The screenshot passed from hand to hand. 'That's so rude,' said Vinod. 'I'd block him.' Nobody asked what Pradeep had written first; it was cropped out. At lunch, Chaitanya watched Sameer do the same thing at the other end of the canteen, his own screenshot, his own crowd. 'He's acting like a victim,' someone said there. By evening there were two groups, and new grievances too: Sameer had 'always' been selfish, Pradeep had 'always' been dramatic. Chaitanya had seen both chats and knew each group had seen only half. He kept quiet, and felt bad about it.

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya first see Pradeep show the screenshot?
qa.a: At the bus stand in Hassan.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya feel bad about keeping quiet?
qa.a: He knew each group had seen only half the chat, and staying silent let the sides harden when he could have added the missing context.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya do now to help?
qa.a: He could tell each group they've seen only one side and encourage Pradeep and Sameer to talk directly instead of polling others.

qa.q: How does the advice from each crowd affect Pradeep and Sameer?
qa.a: Hearing only their own version backed up, each feels more justified and more wronged, so the conflict firms up and gains new grievances.

grounding: A classmate watches two friends each show a cropped chat to their own crowd, who call the other rude, take sides and add new grievances.

passage: Nadia noticed the screenshots before she understood the fight. In the locker hallway of their Vancouver school, Xin was showing her phone to four girls. 'She said "whatever" and then THIS.' 'Wow, that's rude,' said one. 'Honestly, drop her,' said another. Nadia had also seen Chloe, an hour earlier in the library, showing the same chat to her own friends, scrolled to a different part. 'She's so passive-aggressive,' they'd agreed. Now each group was adding things: Xin had forgotten Chloe's birthday in Grade 8; Chloe always made everything about herself. None of that was in the chat. Nadia watched a small text mix-up grow into two teams, and she felt sad, as if she was watching a friendship being quietly buried.

qa.q: Where was Xin showing her phone?
qa.a: In the locker hallway of their Vancouver school.

qa.q: Why did Nadia feel sad watching the two groups?
qa.a: She could see a small text mix-up turning into two teams with new grievances, and it felt like watching a friendship being quietly buried 😔.

qa.q: What might help more than showing the chat to more friends?
qa.a: Xin and Chloe talking to each other directly, or a friend who has seen both sides encouraging that, rather than collecting one-sided verdicts.

qa.q: How does each group's advice change the conflict?
qa.a: Since they hear only one version, they declare the other rude and add old complaints, making the fight bigger than the original messages.

grounding: A classmate observes two girls showing the chat to separate friend groups who call it rude, take sides and pile on old grievances.

passage:
In the school library, Harsha sat at the end of the long table pretending to read. Three tables over, Zainab was holding out her phone to four girls. "Look what Anya sent me."
"That's so rude," said one.
"She's always like that," said another. "Screenshot it for the group."
Harsha had seen Anya's side at lunch, in the canteen, a different phone with a different crowd saying Zainab was the rude one. Harsha thought about saying, "You've both only heard half." Instead, Harsha looked at the page and kept quiet as the new screenshot went round.
By the end of the period, Zainab's friends had a new list of things Anya had done wrong.

qa.q: How many girls was Zainab showing her phone to?
qa.a: Four girls.

qa.q: What might Harsha have been feeling while pretending to read?
qa.a: Harsha was probably uneasy and torn, knowing both sides were hearing only half but unsure about speaking up.

qa.q: What could Harsha do that would help rather than add fuel?
qa.a: Gently say that each group only heard one version, or suggest Zainab talk to Anya directly.

qa.q: What is it like for Zainab as her friends call Anya rude?
qa.a: Zainab likely feels backed up and justified, which makes her more certain and more hurt.

grounding: Shows a classmate watching each side show screenshots to friends who call it rude and take sides, firming up the conflict.

passage:
Dear Vijay bhaiya,
You asked about the drama in my class. It's getting worse, and I'm just watching.
It started with Riddhi and Mansi texting about a cancelled plan. Now both have shown the chat to everyone. At break, Riddhi's group says Mansi was rude. At lunch, Mansi's group says Riddhi started it. Nobody has seen both screenshots together except me, because both of them showed me.
Each group adds new things. "She also ignored you at the fair." "She never shares notes." Stuff that has nothing to do with the chat.
I feel sick about it. They were best friends a week ago. I don't know whether to say something or stay out of it. What would you do?
Ankita

qa.q: What were Riddhi and Mansi texting about at the start?
qa.a: A cancelled plan.

qa.q: What is Ankita feeling while watching the conflict grow?
qa.a: Ankita feels sick and torn, worried about the friendship and unsure whether to speak up.

qa.q: What small step could Ankita take at this stage?
qa.a: Suggest that Riddhi and Mansi talk to each other directly, since only Ankita has seen both sides and the groups keep adding fuel.

qa.q: How are Riddhi and Mansi each affected by their groups' opinions?
qa.a: Each is told they are right and the other is rude, which hardens their positions and adds new grievances.

grounding: Shows a classmate writing about watching two friends show their chat to others, whose one-sided opinions firm up the conflict.

passage:
You want to know how it got so big? I'll tell you, because I watched it all. I'm Farida, and I sit between Rekha and Lipika in class.
It was one chat. Rekha wrote something short, Lipika replied something shorter. By lunch, Rekha had shown it to her whole bench. "That's so rude!" they said. By last period, Lipika had shown her version to the basketball team. "She's so fake!" they said.
And each group added more. Someone remembered Rekha didn't invite Lipika to a birthday two years ago. Someone said Lipika laughed at Rekha's haircut. None of it was in the chat. I kept thinking, nobody has heard both sides. But I didn't say it.

qa.q: Where does Farida sit in class?
qa.a: Between Rekha and Lipika.

qa.q: How can you tell Farida felt uneasy watching this?
qa.a: Farida kept thinking nobody had heard both sides but stayed silent, which suggests Farida felt uncomfortable and stuck.

qa.q: What could Farida have done to slow the conflict?
qa.a: Pointed out that both groups had only heard one version, and encouraged Rekha and Lipika to talk to each other.

qa.q: What is Rekha experiencing as her bench calls Lipika rude?
qa.a: Rekha likely feels supported and more certain she was wronged, while old grievances make her more hurt.

grounding: Shows a classmate watching each girl show the chat to her own group, whose one-sided opinions add new grievances.

passage: I sit between Jagdish and Kiran in the physics lab, so I saw all of it. On Monday morning Jagdish was passing his phone along the back bench: a screenshot of Kiran's messages, the "whatever" circled in red. "That's so rude," Aman said, and two others nodded. By lunch Kiran had a screenshot too, of Jagdish's reply, shown round the canteen table. "He's always like this," someone said, though as far as I know they've barely spoken to him. By Wednesday it wasn't about the cancelled plan anymore. People were bringing up a cricket match from last year and a charger never returned. Kiran looked tired and kept checking the phone. Jagdish laughed too loudly. I don't know what either of them really felt. I only know nobody told them to talk to each other.

qa.q: What was circled in red on Jagdish's screenshot?
qa.a: The "whatever" in Kiran's messages was circled in red.

qa.q: What does the narrator seem to feel while watching this unfold?
qa.a: The narrator seems uneasy and a little sad, noticing the quarrel grow while nobody tells the two of them to talk.

qa.q: How could a friend help instead of taking sides?
qa.a: A friend could say they have heard only one version and suggest Jagdish and Kiran talk to each other directly.

qa.q: What is it like for Kiran as the screenshots spread?
qa.a: Kiran looks tired and keeps checking the phone, perhaps feeling judged by people who heard only one side.

grounding: Shows each side sharing screenshots with friends who call the other rude, so one-sided advice hardens the conflict and adds new grievances.
